medical.title: One body, two systems: Integrating dental and medical care dramatically improves dental follow-up
Electronic health record algorithm can identify drug-resistant epilepsy
medical.summary: An electronic health record (EHR) algorithm can identify people with drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE), according to a study published in the December issue of Epilepsy & Behavior.

medical.title: Multidisciplinary intervention improves fatigue for lymphoma survivors
medical.summary: For lymphoma survivors with persistent fatigue, a multidisciplinary intervention improves fatigue, and the effect is maintained to six months, according to a study published online Nov. 20 in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.

medical.title: World’s largest trial of robotic knee replacement reveals surprising results
medical.summary: Robot-assisted knee replacement surgery offers greater surgical precision, but a landmark clinical trial has revealed a surprising limitation. Despite the advanced technology, patients experienced no meaningful improvements in pain, mobility, or recovery compared with conventional surgery after one year.

medical.title: Half of adults in long COVID study report difficulty breathing 4 years later
medical.summary: Half of adults in a new long COVID study reported symptoms that suggested dysfunctional breathing more than four years after their initial infection. Those with persistent breathing problems tended to be younger and female, and they were less likely to be hospitalized during acute COVID infection.

medical.title: Ecuadorian plant shows potential to control bacteria in food
medical.summary: A plant traditionally used by Indigenous communities in Ecuador could have a new application: helping control bacteria in ready-to-eat foods. A study published in the journal Foods found that extracts of Piper carpunya, locally known as guaviduca, reduced the presence of Clostridium perfringens in a refrigerated risotto food model.

medical.title: Culturally relevant nutrition interventions can engage Black adults more effectively
medical.summary: A recent study in the Journal of Nutrition Education and Behavior explored how researchers can better engage Black adults with hypertension in digital nutrition interventions designed to improve dietary habits and reduce cardiovascular risk.

medical.title: Scientists discover a surprising twist in how the body burns calories
medical.summary: Researchers have discovered that a drug can significantly increase the body's energy expenditure without clearly activating calorie-burning brown fat. The unexpected finding reveals a new challenge in developing obesity treatments that harness the body's natural fat-burning machinery.

science.title: Sending an Australian astronaut to space is expensive. How do we work out if it's worth it?
science.summary: Australia is currently in talks with the European Space Agency (ESA) over potentially flying Katherine Bennell-Pegg on a future space mission. If accepted, Bennell-Pegg—who is the director of space technology at the Australian Space Agency and completed ESA training in 2024—would become the first officially funded Australian astronaut.

science.title: New eyes in the sky make timber harvesting and forest conservation easier and more efficient
science.summary: Flying thousands of feet above northern and eastern Maine, Dave Sandilands searched for illegally dumped trash. On behalf of the New England Forestry Foundation, the University of Maine pilot was surveying both the 760,000-acre (308,000-hectare) Pingree Easement in northern Maine, home to the state's most productive peregrine falcon nesting area, and 335,000 acres (136,000 hectares) in Washington County through the Downeast Lakes Forestry Partnership.

science.title: Scientists discover mysterious lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea
science.summary: More than a mile beneath the surface of the Red Sea, scientists have discovered rare underwater lakes that could reveal secrets about Earth's ancient oceans and the possibility of alien life. Known as brine pools, these extremely salty, oxygen-free environments are surprisingly teeming with microbial life, challenging our understanding of where living organisms can survive.

science.title: Do we really know more about space than the ocean?
science.summary: New discoveries are made about the world every day—a species of deep-sea fish here, a new galaxy there. There's a saying, "We know more about space than the ocean." But is this true? How do we determine knowing? Is it the number of things we have directly observed, or is it a matter of resolution?

science.title: Astronomers may have discovered a black hole born before the first stars
science.summary: A mysterious object named Phoebe, detected when it briefly magnified a distant star, could be a primordial black hole formed just after the Big Bang. With an estimated mass only three times that of the Moon, it may be a 13-billion-year-old cosmic relic that offers new clues to the mystery of dark matter.

science.title: Disliking AI doesn't deter its influence
science.summary: An aversion to artificial intelligence (AI) does not lessen the influence of the technology on people and their decision-making, according to new research from City St George's, University of London.

science.title: Giant deer bones may push human arrival in Ireland back by 1,000 years
science.summary: A team of archaeologists and scientists has uncovered tantalizing new evidence that Late Upper Paleolithic hunter-gatherers may have lived in southern Ireland around 13,500 years ago—nearly a millennium earlier than currently confirmed.

science.title: Fermented milk may have held ritual power in Neolithic Denmark
science.summary: Experimental archaeology sheds light on the substances fermented in Neolithic Scandinavian pottery and deposited in tombs, suggesting fermented dairy products held symbolic significance in prehistoric funerary rituals.

environment.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
environment.summary: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.

environment.title: Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel
environment.summary: Scientists have developed an efficient method to transform used coffee grounds into a potential source of biodiesel while preserving the leftover material for other renewable fuels and valuable chemicals. The discovery could turn millions of tons of discarded coffee waste into a surprisingly useful resource for sustainable energy.

environment.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
environment.summary: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

environment.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

environment.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
environment.summary: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.

mix_items.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
mix_items.summary: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel

The discovery could turn millions of tons of discarded coffee waste into a surprisingly useful resource for sustainable energy.

mix_items.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
mix_items.summary: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

mix_items.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

mix_items.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
mix_items.summary: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.
